session.context:
pqac-0adcec25: The excerpt is a protocol for evaluating Japan’s nationwide Specific Health Check-ups (SHC), introduced in 2008 for primary prevention of obesity-related diseases including diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia. It states that effectiveness has not yet been systematically evaluated. The planned study uses an employment-based health insurance database and target trial emulation. Eligible participants are adults aged 40–74 without baseline diagnoses of hypertension or diabetes, and SHC recipients will be compared with non-recipients. Follow-up is up to 10 years, and the main outcome is the 10-year incidence of diabetes/hypertension analyzed with pooled logistic regression. No hazard ratios are reported in this excerpt.
From Masato Takeuchi, Tomohiro Shinozaki, and Koji Kawakami. Effectiveness of specific health check-ups in japan for the primary prevention of obesity-related diseases: a protocol for a target trial emulation. BMJ Open, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2022-070417, doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2022-070417.

pqac-147ba6d6: The paper is a protocol for a target trial emulation evaluating Japan’s nationwide Specific Health Check-ups (SHC) program for primary prevention of obesity-related diseases. It uses an employment-based health insurance database with claims and SHC receipt/non-receipt records. Eligible participants are adults aged 40–74 without baseline diagnosed hypertension or diabetes and with no prior SHC history at baseline. Participants are followed up to 10 years, and the 10-year incidence of diabetes/hypertension is compared between SHC recipients and non-recipients using pooled logistic regression adjusted for baseline confounders. The abstract does not report hazard ratios or results; it describes planned analyses and sensitivity analyses.
From Masato Takeuchi, Tomohiro Shinozaki, and Koji Kawakami. Effectiveness of specific health check-ups in japan for the primary prevention of obesity-related diseases: a protocol for a target trial emulation. BMJ Open, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2022-070417, doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2022-070417.

pqac-55aff9b8: The excerpt describes a large 7-year prospective cohort study of about 0.5 million Chinese adults that included physical measurements and blood tests at baseline, with subsequent tracking of health outcomes. It reports that among people without diabetes at baseline, daily fresh fruit consumption was associated with a 12% lower relative risk of incident diabetes versus never/rarely consuming fruit. Among participants with pre-existing diabetes, eating fresh fruit more than 3 days per week was linked to a 17% lower all-cause mortality risk and 13%–28% lower risk of diabetic vascular complications. The text frames these as inverse associations relevant to diabetes prevention and secondary prevention.
From Huaidong Du, Liming Li, Derrick Bennett, Yu Guo, Iain Turnbull, Ling Yang, Fiona Bragg, Zheng Bian, Yiping Chen, Junshi Chen, Iona Y. Millwood, Sam Sansome, Liangcai Ma, Ying Huang, Ningmei Zhang, Xiangyang Zheng, Qiang Sun, Timothy J. Key, Rory Collins, Richard Peto, and Zhengming Chen. Fresh fruit consumption in relation to incident diabetes and diabetic vascular complications: a 7-y prospective study of 0.5 million chinese adults. PLoS Medicine, 2017. URL: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1002279, doi:10.1371/journal.pmed.1002279.

pqac-c72b815c: The excerpt is about a Korean adult cohort from KNHANES VII (2016–2018) examining dietary sodium-to-potassium ratio and cardiometabolic risk factors, not Japan’s Specific Health Check-up data. It reports no overall significant association with hypertension, obesity, or diabetes in all participants, but in adults aged ≥65 years the high Na/K group had higher hypertension risk versus low Na/K (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.10–1.72). Higher Na/K was also associated with metabolic syndrome and some components. No hazard ratios for incident diabetes, hypertension, or hyperlipidaemia from Japanese health check-up data are provided.
From Seo-Young Baek and Hye-Kyeong Kim. Association of dietary sodium-to-potassium ratio with cardiometabolic risk factors in korean adults: findings from the korean national health and nutrition examination survey. Nutrients, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/nu15143134, doi:10.3390/nu15143134.

pqac-19f1da36: The excerpt is about a 2022 cross-sectional study in a Chinese health check-up population examining the association between serum uric acid/HDL-cholesterol ratio (UHR) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). It included 19,458 participants from annual health check-ups in Nanjing in 2019. The main outcome was CKD defined by eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m². The results reported a negative correlation between UHR and eGFR and a higher CKD risk in the highest UHR quartile (OR=9.28). This excerpt does not mention incident diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, cohort hazard ratios, or other specific health check-up outcomes.
From Yang Cheng, Hao Zhang, Hui Zheng, Hongli Yin, Ying Wang, Hui Wang, Liubao Gu, and Donghua Yin. contexts.context: This excerpt is about osteoporosis, not health check-ups or incident diabetes/hypertension/hyperlipidaemia hazard ratios. It reports a retrospective cohort study using NHANES data (2005–2010, 2013–2014) on 801 osteoporosis patients followed until 2015. The study examined history of fractures and hypertension in relation to all-cause death. Fracture history was associated with increased mortality risk (RR 1.502), including spine fracture (RR 2.944) and hip fracture (RR 2.033). Hypertension alone was not significantly associated with mortality, but there was a significant positive interaction between fractures and hypertension (AP 0.456).

contexts.context: The excerpt is a 2023 retrospective cohort study of male patients with type 2 diabetes in Taiwan examining whether metformin use affects the risk of lower urinary tract symptoms/benign prostatic hyperplasia (LUTS/BPH). It reports propensity-score matched ever vs never users of metformin and hazard ratios for LUTS/BPH incidence, including dose- and duration-related analyses. The abstract does not mention health check-ups, incident diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, or hazard ratios for those outcomes. The key finding is a lower LUTS/BPH risk with metformin (HR 0.69), with stronger reductions at higher cumulative duration/dose.

contexts.context: The paper is a protocol for a target trial emulation evaluating Japan’s nationwide Specific Health Check-ups (SHC) program for primary prevention of obesity-related diseases. It uses an employment-based health insurance database with claims and SHC receipt/non-receipt records. Eligible participants are adults aged 40–74 without baseline diagnosed hypertension or diabetes and with no prior SHC history at baseline. Participants are followed up to 10 years, and the 10-year incidence of diabetes/hypertension is compared between SHC recipients and non-recipients using pooled logistic regression adjusted for baseline confounders. The abstract does not report hazard ratios or results; it describes planned analyses and sensitivity analyses.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a 2023 retrospective study of 933 asymptomatic people undergoing colonoscopy to identify predictors of colorectal polyps. It reports that age over 40, male sex, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) >1.435 ng/mL were independent risk factors for colorectal polyps; CEA >1.435 ng/mL was also an independent predictor for adenomas. Other labs such as uric acid, glycosylated hemoglobin, fasting blood glucose, triglycerides, total cholesterol, and HDL were compared across groups, but no independent risk factors were found for adenoma number. The paper focuses on colorectal lesions, not health-check-up hazard ratios for diabetes, hypertension, or hyperlipidaemia.

contexts.context: The excerpt is a 2022 Japanese multicenter retrospective cohort study about cancer patients receiving drug therapy for diabetes. It reports that among 131,701 cancer patients, 6,135 had coexisting diabetes. Patients with diabetes had worse 5-year survival (56.2% vs 72.7%) and a higher risk of second primary cancer (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.08–1.41). It also mentions site-specific increased risks for multiple myeloma, uterus, pancreas, and liver cancers. The study uses cancer registry and administrative data from Osaka Prefecture and evaluates diabetes at cancer diagnosis, but it does not discuss health check-up incident diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, or their hazard ratios.

contexts.context: The excerpt is about a Chinese prospective cohort study on fresh fruit consumption and diabetes outcomes, not a Japan-specific health check-up study. It reports that among people free of diabetes at baseline, daily fresh fruit intake was associated with a 12% lower relative risk of incident diabetes versus never/rarely eating fruit. Among those with pre-existing diabetes, eating fruit more than three days per week was linked to a 17% lower all-cause mortality risk and 13%–28% lower risk of diabetic vascular complications. No information is provided about Japanese specific health check-up data, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, or hazard ratios for those outcomes.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: What hazard ratios were observed for incident diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia after receiving Specific Health check-ups?

I cannot answer. The provided context describes a protocol for a target trial emulation of Japan’s Specific Health Check-ups and explicitly states that no hazard ratios or results were reported in the excerpt. It only specifies planned analyses of the 10-year incidence of diabetes and hypertension using pooled logistic regression, and it does not provide any observed hazard ratios for incident diabetes, hypertension, or hyperlipidaemia after receiving Specific Health Check-ups.
